summary.text: James Talarico is the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Texas and a state representative first elected in 2018. A former public school teacher with degrees from the University of Texas at Austin and Harvard, he won the March 2026 Democratic primary over U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett and faces Republican Ken Paxton in November.
His campaign describes him as an eighth-generation Texan and Presbyterian seminarian, and he says he has never taken corporate PAC money.

paragraphs.text: James Talarico was born in Round Rock, Texas, attended Wells Branch Elementary School and graduated from McNeil High School.
He earned a bachelor's degree in government from the University of Texas at Austin and a master's degree in education policy from Harvard University.
He then taught sixth-grade language arts at Rhodes Middle School on the west side of San Antonio, which he describes as one of the poorest ZIP codes in Texas.
Talarico first ran for the Texas House in 2018 and, by his account, flipped a district that Donald Trump had won two years earlier.
He later represented House District 50, winning re-election in 2022 and 2024, and sits on the Public Education, Juvenile Justice and Family Issues, and Calendars committees.

His office says he helped write a reform of the state's school finance system in his first term and passed legislation capping insulin copays at $25 a month, importing lower-cost prescription drugs from Canada, and capping Pre-K class sizes; he is a type 1 diabetic.
Texas Monthly named him one of the ten best legislators, according to the House biography.
Talarico ran for U.S. Senate in 2026 and won the March 3 Democratic primary with 52.4% of the vote, ahead of Jasmine Crockett (46.2%) and Ahmad Hassan (1.3%).
His general-election opponent is Ken Paxton, who defeated incumbent John Cornyn in the Republican primary runoff.

Talarico says he has passed 60 bipartisan bills, including measures on prescription drug costs and child care, and that the central divide in the country is between the top and the bottom rather than left and right.
